notes.b: Home management means organising time, money, energy and effort to run the household efficiently. Technology contributes by cutting the work, time and energy a task needs and by improving the result, as appliances and home systems take over repetitive tasks.
points: Washing machines, dishwashers, vacuum cleaners and food processors replace hand washing, drying, sweeping and food preparation, so these tasks are less labour-intensive and take less time.
Because tasks finish quickly, time is freed for family, leisure, study or paid work, which improves the quality of home life.
Automatic programmes and timers let a task run unsupervised, so the household can do other work or rest while it runs.
Steam cleaners clean and sanitise floors, carpets and upholstery with little or no chemical cleaner, helping to remove dirt and bacteria and improving hygiene.
Easy-care products, such as non-iron and stain-resistant fabrics, non-stick surfaces and smooth wipe-clean worktops, need less washing, ironing and upkeep.
Technology can increase the effectiveness of some tasks: steam cleaning lifts dirt that a dry cloth leaves behind, and a dishwasher washes at a higher temperature than hands can bear.
notes.tip: Pair each technology with its benefit in one developed sentence, for example a steam cleaner and the hygiene it gives, and vary your examples across laundry, cleaning and cooking rather than giving five kitchen ones. Do not claim steam cleaners kill all germs or need no chemicals at all.

notes.b: Heating, hot water and appliances are a large part of household running costs. Technology lets the household use energy only where and when it is needed, which lowers fuel bills.
points: Programmable timers switch heating and hot water on only when needed, reducing fuel use and bills.

Zoned heating uses separate controls (thermostats or thermostatic radiator valves) to heat different parts of the house to different temperatures, so unused rooms are not heated; this gives comfort where needed and lower fuel bills.

Microcomputer chips (microprocessors) in appliances such as washing machines, cookers, microwaves and heating systems sense load, temperature or time and adjust the programme, so the energy and water used are matched to the task.
Microwave ovens heat small and medium portions faster than a conventional oven, so they use less energy for reheating and defrosting.
Appliances with a high energy-label class are cheaper to run. LED lighting and standby-saving features also cut electricity use.
Solar panels turn sunlight into electricity (photovoltaic) or heat water (solar thermal), reducing the household's reliance on mains energy.
notes.tip: Name the technology and then the effect, for example timers on heating switch it on only when needed, lowering fuel bills. Give no figures for how much money or energy is saved.

notes.b: Technology protects the home from intruders and its users from accidents, often without anyone having to pay constant attention. This gives security and peace of mind.
points: Burglar alarms sound on forced entry and can alert occupants or a monitoring service.
CCTV cameras record the outside of the home, deterring intruders and providing evidence after an incident.
Automated security lighting switches on when movement or darkness is detected, making the outside of the home less attractive to intruders.
Entry-phones and video doorbells let residents check who is at the door before opening it.
Electronic gates can be opened and closed remotely, so residents do not have to leave a vehicle to enter the property.
Built-in safety devices such as automatic cut-outs, thermostats, door interlocks and child locks in appliances protect users from hazards without relying on constant attention.
A residual current device (RCD) in the fuse board cuts the power when a fault occurs, and smoke and carbon monoxide alarms warn occupants of danger.
notes.tip: Security systems that deter burglary and built-in safety devices are both accepted as ways technology contributes to efficient home management. Give a named device and what it does.

notes.b: Computers, phones and the internet let a household keep in touch, manage money and find information without leaving the house. This saves travel time and cost.
points: Mobile phones, email, video calling and messaging keep family members in touch quickly across distances. Social media likewise keeps household members in contact and shares information quickly.
The household can get information and services without travelling, for example recipes, product reviews and consumer information from the internet.
Online and mobile banking let bills be paid and balances checked at any time without visiting a branch.
Budgeting and accounting software or apps record income and spending by category and help the household plan future expenditure.
Internet shopping allows goods to be compared and bought without travelling to shops, and price comparison finds the best deal.
Computers let some members work or study from home, which can reduce commuting time and cost.
Smartphone apps in a smart home can turn lights, heating or appliances on or off, and check their status, from outside the home.
notes.tip: Communication technology that speeds up information, and mobile phones used for paying bills, are accepted answers. Use the generic terms video calling and messaging apps rather than naming a product.

notes.b: Technology is not all benefit. A balanced answer also weighs what it costs and what can go wrong, which earns extra credit at Higher Level.
points: The initial cost must be weighed against savings in time, energy and effort over the life of the product. Running costs, repair costs and replacement when machines fail must be added.
Electronic appliances need electricity to operate, so a power cut or breakdown stops the task.
Components of electronic appliances may need a qualified person to repair them, so spare parts and servicing must be available.
Internet-connected devices hold personal data and need secure passwords and regular software updates to resist misuse.
Heavy screen use can reduce the time a family spends together.
Manufacture, energy use and the disposal of electrical waste have effects on the environment.
notes.tip: At Higher Level, add one balanced drawback to your answer, such as cost, dependence on electricity, repair or data security, rather than claiming technology only has benefits.

notes.h: Answering questions on technology in the home
notes.b: Questions on this topic ask how technology helps the household run efficiently. The same answer pattern works whether you are asked to state or to discuss.
points: Use the pattern of a point, a named technology and the benefit, for example timers on heating switch it on only when needed, lowering fuel bills.

Ordinary Level asks you to state three ways, so give any three with a short example, such as appliances saving time and labour, zoned heating, steam cleaners for hygiene, security systems or communication saving time.
Higher Level asks you to discuss, so give five developed points spread across workload, time, quality of life, easy-care products, effectiveness, computer-controlled energy saving and security.
Tie examples to a task such as laundry, cleaning, cooking, heating, security, money or communication.
notes.tip: Name the technology and then the benefit, vary the areas rather than giving five kitchen examples, keep each point to one developed sentence, and at Higher Level add one drawback.

keyTerms.definition: A heating system with separate controls that heat different parts of a building to different temperatures.
A control that switches an appliance or heating system on and off at set times.
A cleaning appliance that uses hot steam to loosen dirt and sanitise surfaces with little or no chemical cleaner.
A system that detects forced entry into a building and gives a warning signal.
Closed-circuit television, in which cameras transmit images to a recorder or monitor that only authorised users can see.
A panel of photovoltaic cells that converts sunlight into electricity, or a collector that heats water from sunlight.
Managing bank accounts, paying bills and transferring money through a secure internet connection.
A computer package that records income and expenditure so the household can plan and monitor its spending.
An appliance connected to the internet or a home network, so that it can be monitored or controlled remotely.
A product designed to need little washing, ironing or maintenance during use.

factCards.term: Four ways technology reduces household workload
factCards.definition: Appliances replace manual tasks, automatic programmes run unattended, steam cleaners speed up cleaning, and easy-care products need less upkeep.
It heats only occupied rooms, lets each area be kept at a comfortable temperature, and reduces wasted fuel.
Burglar alarms, CCTV, automated security lighting and remotely controlled electronic gates.

factCards.term: Three uses of computers in managing a home
factCards.definition: Budgeting and accounting software, online banking and online shopping.

factCards.term: Three ways technology improves household communication
factCards.definition: Email, video calling and social media let members keep in touch quickly across distances.

factCards.term: Two ways automated lighting and heating are controlled from a distance
factCards.definition: Smartphone apps connected to the home network, and timers or sensors that switch devices on automatically.

questions.prompt: Outline three ways in which technological developments have made the management of a home more efficient.
questions.model: Any three, each with a short example. Appliances and timers reduce the time and effort needed for household tasks, for example a dishwasher or a timer on a washing machine. Energy-efficient technology such as zoned heating or programmable controls lowers fuel and electricity bills. Security technology such as burglar alarms, CCTV and automated lighting protects the home. Computer packages and online banking and shopping save time and help with budgeting. Smart apps let the household control heating and lights remotely.

questions.prompt: Evaluate how household technology contributes to the efficient management of the home, giving examples of appliances and home systems that save time, energy and money.
questions.model: Workload: appliances such as washing machines, dishwashers and vacuum cleaners reduce the time and labour of routine tasks, and steam cleaners improve hygiene. Automatic programmes let tasks run unattended. Energy and cost: timers, zoned heating and chip-controlled appliances reduce fuel and electricity use, and solar panels reduce reliance on mains energy. Security: burglar alarms, CCTV, automated lighting and electronic gates protect the home and can be operated remotely. Money and communication: budgeting software, online banking and internet shopping help plan spending and save travel, while email, video calls and social media keep the household connected. Evaluation: the benefits depend on the initial cost of the technology, the need for electricity and servicing, and the security of personal data on connected devices, so the household should weigh these against the savings the technology gives.
